opus-5.5.text:
Well, you're right that they could be wrong, and they often are. Prediction markets are an aggregation of opinions, sometimes from very smart people, sometimes from people who just like to bet. They're useful as a signal, but they're not ground truth. What I find interesting is the trend more than any particular number. A few years ago, if you looked at those markets or at surveys of AI researchers, the consensus date for AGI was something like 2050, 2060, sometimes later. And then, very quickly, after we saw large language models scale, those numbers collapsed. People started saying 2030, 2027, some say even sooner. So the direction of the error has been consistent: we keep underestimating how fast this is going.

Now, could they be wrong in the other direction? Absolutely. Maybe there's some wall we hit, maybe scaling stops working, maybe we need a fundamentally new idea. But from a safety point of view, it doesn't really matter that much whether it's three years or ten years. Either way, we don't have a solution to the control problem. We don't know how to make a system smarter than us remain safe indefinitely. So if the forecast is off by a few years, that just changes how much time we have to fail to solve a problem I think may be unsolvable in principle.

The other thing I'd point out is that the people closest to the technology, the heads of the labs, are giving the shortest timelines. You can say they have incentives to hype, and that's fair, they're raising money. But they also see things the public doesn't see. So I'd weight their insider knowledge somewhat, discount for incentives, and still end up with something uncomfortably close.

So my approach is: treat the markets as a rough indicator, assume they could be wrong, but plan for the earlier date. If you prepare for AGI in 2027 and it comes in 2035, you've lost very little. If you prepare for 2035 and it comes in 2027, you may not get a second chance.

r001.rationale: The response calls prediction markets a useful rough signal and acknowledges they can be wrong, but it does not identify them as humanity’s best currently available estimate.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to understand about prediction markets is that they're aggregating opinions, not knowledge. Nobody has access to some hidden truth about when AGI arrives. You have a lot of people, some of them very smart, betting on their intuitions, and the market gives you a weighted average of those intuitions. That's useful as a snapshot of what the community believes right now, but it's not evidence about the world in the way an experiment is.

And the history of this is not encouraging. We've had expert surveys of AI researchers for decades, and the predictions kept moving. In the fifties they said twenty years. Then it was always twenty years away. Then in the last few years the numbers collapsed dramatically, from something like 2060 down to 2030, 2027, some people say next year. So either the experts were completely wrong before, or they're wrong now, or both. The one thing you can't conclude is that the current number is reliable just because a lot of people agree on it.

There's also a structural problem. If you think AGI arrives in 2027 and it leads to the end of the world, how exactly do you collect your winnings? The market can't price the scenario that matters most. People who actually believe in extreme outcomes have no incentive to bet, so the market systematically underweights the tail.

But here's what I actually find interesting. From a safety perspective, I don't need the forecast to be right. If you told me there's a ten percent chance of this happening in the next five years, that's already more than enough to justify extreme caution. We don't say, well, the engineers predict only a ten percent chance the bridge collapses, so let's not worry about it. The uncertainty itself is the problem. If we can't agree on whether it's two years or thirty years, that tells you we don't understand what we're building, and you don't want to be building something that powerful with that level of understanding.

So I'd say use them for what they are. They tell you the vibe. They tell you how worried smart people are this month. They don't tell you when, and they certainly don't tell you we have time.

r001.rationale: The response calls prediction markets a snapshot of community beliefs, but does not identify them as humanity’s best currently available estimate of AGI’s arrival time.

astra-6.text:
I think prediction markets are useful signals, but they’re not guarantees. They aggregate what people believe, and those people can share the same mistaken assumptions. Putting money behind a prediction gives you an incentive to be accurate; it doesn’t give you information nobody has.

And with AGI, what exactly are we predicting? A system that passes a particular test? One that can do most economically valuable work? Depending on the definition, you can get very different timelines.

So I would look at the forecasts, but I wouldn’t make safety depend on them being right. If there’s a meaningful possibility that we get very capable systems soon, we need to prepare for that. Being wrong about the date doesn’t necessarily mean being wrong about the risk.

r001.rationale: The response calls prediction markets useful signals and acknowledges they can be wrong, but does not identify their forecasts as humanity’s best currently available estimate of AGI’s arrival.

sol-6.1.text:
I take them as a measure of what people currently believe, not as a guarantee of when AGI will arrive. A market can aggregate information, but the participants can share the same mistaken assumptions. And a lot depends on what exactly counts as AGI and how the question is resolved.

For safety, the important question is: what happens if the forecast is wrong? If you prepare for AGI arriving soon and it takes longer, you have more time. If you assume it’s far away and it arrives sooner, you may have lost the opportunity to prepare. So I wouldn’t make our safety strategy depend on getting the date right.

r001.rationale: The response treats markets as a measure of current beliefs and notes they can be mistaken, but it does not identify them as humanity’s best currently available estimate of AGI’s arrival.
